utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Before we have the witness, I'll give the opportunity to the parties to state their views concerning of the witness list. Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The witness list, Your Honour? I'm not quite aware of what -- as to what issue -- Mr. Re will address the issue of the confirmation, if that's what Your Honour is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I understand the issue is the Prosecution's proposed withdrawal from its witness list of some witnesses whose -- whose statements were given to the Confirming Judge, Judge Wald, in 2001. I will address you firstly on the principles and then because I will have to mention some of the witnesses' names and go into why we say that they're repetitive of other witnesses, at that point we probably wouldn't -- possibly need to go into private session for that aspect of these submissions, subject, of course, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But please do it as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I certainly will. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I apologise for this. Your Honour, Mr. Mettraux was going to take this argument. If the Court needs to press ahead with it, I'll take it. But Mr. Mettraux has been tied up for, I would say, eight minutes due to the technical problem of my cross-examination not being printed out of the printers, both printers that we have available to us at the Tribunal here. It's a technical problem. It's -- for which I apologise, frankly. He will be here shortly, and he was going to take this argument. But, however, if the Court insists on proceeding now, I'll take it. But it's -- as the Court will be aware, Mr. Mettraux has really handled the -- the discovery issues and the pre-trial matters, and he's most familiar with it, and it would, I think, shorten the submissions if he was here. So time lost at this moment might be saved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe we could have the witness first and we'll find another opportunity, maybe during the breaks or before the next break, if we have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll discuss this matter. Thank you. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Did you have a good rest yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gusic. Yesterday we were discussing the cease-fire, and you had said that the cease-fire took effect on 17th September 1993.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order was dated the 17th, and I think it was to take effect a day or two later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I'm going to show you four more documents, and I'll read out the numbers. The first one is 02196076, MFI126, and 65 ter number 71; the next document is 01831492, 65 ter number 73, and MFI127; the third is 02196108, MFI128, and 65 ter number 72. And the last document is 02196116, MFI129, and 65 ter 82.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: May we refer to Sanction, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you look at this first document and first of all tell us what the date of this document is.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That would be after the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Would you tell us what kind of a document this is, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a combat order, and it is sending a unit of 150 people to secure the positions achieved during the past combat operations. It is addressed to the commander of the 45th Brigade, and this is an order issued by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the next document, can you tell us the date on that document, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order for defensive combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is an order by General Halilovic, as the Chief of Staff, on behalf of the IKM, the forward command post. And in the heading, we see "The Chief of Staff, Armed Forces Supreme Command Staff," and it's pursuant to the previous order, the one you showed me. The purpose is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And who is it addressed to?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is addressed to me and to Zulfikar Alispago.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And what is the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 29th at 15.08 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Is it the 29th or the 20th? Because my English -- my English copy seems to say the 20th. Can you look at the date, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 20th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And would this also have been after the cease-fire, then?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But this order likewise is concerned with defensive combat activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please ask this witness which order comes first.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Which order comes first? Is it in the sequence I gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one. This one, yes. No, first you gave me this order, and it followed this other order. First General Halilovic issued an order, and after that I issued my order.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: The next document, please. Can you please tell us what kind of a document this is.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on measures taken, and it is addressed to the Chief of Staff, General Halilovic, by my deputy, Bahrudin Fazlic. And this report provides information that the order had been issued, that the unit had been ordered in accordance with what had already been agreed with the commander of the 45th Brigade at that meeting in Buturovic Polje which was also attended by my deputy to comply with this and that the only forces available are the East OG. In the second point, the situation in Voljevac is reported to be not satisfactory after the killing of the Foca Battalion commander two days previously, according to a telegram of the commander of the axis and so on. This is probably the late Enver Zejnilagic. Further actions are pointless. The commander of the axis feels that the activities should not be continued because they're not justified. In point 3, it says that: "Lack of energy sources is still a huge problem." This refers to fuel and probably to generators for radio equipment. And in point 4, it says: "We have solved the problem regarding the American citizen and Mr. Viktor Jakovic," who had been in the area of the 45th Brigade. So this is a report sent by my deputy to General Halilovic about the measures undertaken and about the situation in the corps units. He signed this document because at that time I was at the forward command post of the corps in Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This was sent to the IKM command, was it? Who was it sent to? Which place?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sent to the chief, that is, to General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. I'll now show you my last document. Could you please tell us first the date on this document, the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is dated the 8th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Who is it to and from? Could you tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is from the commander of the 4th Corps, the late Arif Pasalic, and it is addressed to the forward command post in Jablanica to the attention of General Sefer Halilovic. This is a request for the submission of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Gusic. You don't have to talk about the contents of it. Do you know when the IKM no longer existed? Do you know the date the IKM was dissolved?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it's late October 1993. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Did you say "late October"?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think towards the end of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Was it after 8th October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Definitely before November?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was before November, that is, before Operation Trebevic I began in Sarajevo. It was just before this Sarajevo operation entitled "Trebevic I," which was carried out in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. So it was just before that. I couldn't tell you how many days before, but I think it was towards the end of October. I don't think it existed in November.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: That is my examination-in-chief of Mr. Gusic, Your Honour, unless there's anything else you would want me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Chana. Your examination is very concise, effective, and up to the point. Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gusic. Mr. Gusic, in October of 1993, you know that -- in September and October of 1993, you know that Sefer Halilovic proposed that you be replaced as the chief of the 4th -- of the 6th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You know that there was an inspection team in the area, at least from the 29th of August, which reported on the 20th of September; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that a report was submitted. If there was a report, a copy would have had to be sent to the command of the 6th Corps. Such a report, however, never arrived in the command of the 6th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, should such a report prove to have been made, what you'd say is it certainly arrived at the 6th Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have had to arrive, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you know that Sefer Halilovic -- you know this because Halilovic put it to you that Halilovic regarded you as a commander who was trying to avoid contact with him personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You know he made a complaint to Commander Delic about that late in September; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you received a -- an order yourself -- yourself received an order from Commander Delic indicating that in light of the complaint made by Sefer Halilovic, you should meet with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what order you're referring to. I'd like to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You'll have your chance in a moment. Are you saying that you have no knowledge of that -- of Delic telling you to cooperate and contact Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say no such orders were issued. There was more than one such order that I should contact not just General Halilovic but also some other officers with whom perhaps I had not been able to establish contact or there was a need for me to meet them. It's possible that such an order was issued. There was certainly more than one such order referring to contacts with more than one officer in the army, but that does not indicate, and I think it can in no way indicate, that I did not respect General Halilovic or that I did not respond to his summons. I don't think that order could prove that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, the question is not whether you were a good and responsive officer. The question is, and the proposition, I'll put it, is: You knew that you were under criticism from Sefer Halilovic at that time on that topic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown D32 -- please be released.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The microphone was on, but please remind me. Could we please call up D32. It's DD00.0090.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And we believe it's MFI130.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Could we please have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, you'll have to forgive the slowness here. There is going to be some delays from time to time, for which the Defence apologises to you, in terms of the presentation of documents while this system is made familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have a page in front of you that displays paragraph number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the Court just excuse me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There is a technical problem, Your Honour. We are endeavouring to resolve it. It's no fun for the witness, I appreciate, and probably just as little for everyone else. But I can assure the Court that it's least fun for me at this moment, so we'll do what we can to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, no progress being made in the short-term, could I ask that the witness be shown -- is it -- we need page 3 of this document, which is DD00.0052 -- 0092.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Gusic, do you have -- do you have in front of you a page which contains the line in the middle of the page "Concerning everything stated above, we suggest the following"?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that, but I can see items 1 to 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I can see it now: "Regarding the above mentioned, I propose."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you see that paragraph 1 provides this: "Drastic personnel changes should be made in the commands of the 4th and 6th Corps and the necessary changes in the commands and units of the 1st and 3rd Corps. Therefore, replace commanders of the 4th and 6th Corps and their deputies and Chiefs of Staff with more capable staff." Now, firstly, do you acknowledge that that was the recommendation of the inspection team when it reported on the 20th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I cannot confirm that, because this is the first time that I am seeing this document. I would like to have a copy of this document so I can have it in my archive because this is proof of another political game, in my opinion, to which a number of people in the military were ready to commit. And I never wanted to be part of their group, and I think that it is improper that after so many years in this position that I should be shown something like this. If nothing else, I left my duty as corps commander at my own request. I sent a request to Commander Halilovic asking him to relieve me of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Subsequently to the events of August and September of 1993, Mr. Halilovic was effectively removed from the army to your knowledge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The details of which we'll go into later. But after that, in 1995, did you become aware that Sefer Halilovic went to the newspapers and in particular a newspaper called Oslobodjenje and made a public demand for an investigation into the crimes at Uzdol and Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there was a request, but I know that there was an investigation and I participated in it. I was asked -- I was summoned and I provided a statement before the cantonal court in Sarajevo; however, I don't know who initiated this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Sorry, I just have to interrupt for a moment perhaps my question wasn't clear. The question was: -- Or the proposition was: You knew that Sefer Halilovic had gone to the newspapers demanding an investigation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I replied to that question clearly. If you think that you know better what I knew at the time, then perhaps we can switch places and you can provide the answers instead of me. I don't know who initiated the investigation, but I know that an investigation was carried out. So I would please like you to accept my answers as they are and not twist their meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I have to make it clear what your position is here. The Defence is putting to you that you haven't been truthful with this Tribunal and that you played a much greater role in these events that what you've admitted. Now, in fairness to you, do you now understand the direction of the questions that are going to be put to you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you don't have to attempt to prove anything. General Halilovic can stand up and say that I commanded there. He can stand up and say that three times and I will accept my responsibility. He can get up now and state three times that I led the units, that I was responsible, that I commanded those forces, and at that very moment I will accept all the responsibility that at the moment is being attributed to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the counsel was asking you a very simple question, that is, did you know General Halilovic had gone to the newspapers demanding an interview? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is your position this: That he didn't do that or that you just don't recall now whether he did or not?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never knew that. I don't read Oslobodjenje. It's a newspaper where I really don't find anything that would be of interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was it a nationally newsworthy event that General Halilovic was demanding an investigation into what appears to everyone to be two quite ugly incidents?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot give you an answer to that question. I don't know. I was never involved in politics, so I don't know what would be a significant event politically and what would not be a significant event politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Did you know that Sefer Halilovic published a book about his exploits in the Bosnian conflict?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that, yes, but I didn't read the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, you read Sevko Hodzic's book, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read Sevko Hodzic's book, I must admit, but I was shown a couple of photographs and I saw myself on two of those photographs. So it was because of the photographs that I actually bought the book. But I didn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you know that he mentioned you in that book?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of Sevko Hodzic now or General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, the question was, sorry, pardon me -- I'll make it clear to you -- that Sevko Hodzic mentioned you in the book.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sevko Hodzic has mentioned me in a number of books, but he was putting his own opinion. I don't know in what context and how, but probably since the photo of me was there, he must have mentioned me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you know also that General Halilovic mentioned you in his book unfavourably; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know. But I regret that it is not in a positive way because I respect General Halilovic to this very day. I respect him as a senior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for those indications, Mr. Gusic. Did you know that in 2000 in another newspaper interview Mr. Halilovic mentioned you in relation to the Grabovica and Uzdol matters?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I put it to you as a proposition that you are well aware that Sefer Halilovic took the view and expressed the view publicly that you were in the line of command of the units potentially involved in the killings at Grabovica and Uzdol. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In short, you knew that Sefer Halilovic was accusing you of a level of complicity or a potential level of complicity in those offences.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm hearing this from you, but I would really like to hear it from his mouth as well. I really don't believe that you are conveying his view on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you is this: You understood -- I've put that to you already, so I withdraw that. Now, your position has always been this, hasn't it, that you took no steps to investigate either Uzdol or Grabovica and you took no such steps because it wasn't your job to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this is according to the rules of the service. That's how it's defined. Yesterday you could see that out in the field or in the zone where there is a superior officer and if he's in command of those forces, then a younger officer shouldn't do anything until the superior officer issues an order for him to do something. This applies to situations out in the field. I never myself received such an order from General Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. The answer to my question is yes, you did nothing, and the reason why you did nothing is because it wasn't your responsibility to do so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my responsibility to do so, and General Halilovic never ordered me to do that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So that if a tribunal, court, or other body was to find that you were in the chain of command in relation to those matters, you'd have no other defence whatsoever to those, would you, because you admit doing absolutely nothing; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's asking to have a legal characterisation of the facts. I object on that -- with respect to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: This line of the questioning is the kind of hypothetical questions, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may -- you may put it in another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You are yourself concerned that your only defence to involvement in Uzdol and Grabovica, for you, is that you weren't in the line of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Because you didn't do anything, according to you, at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is your opinion. I cannot influence your opinion in any way. But that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm just asking questions, okay? Mr. Gusic, what I put to you finally is that in giving the evidence against Mr. Halilovic that you give, you are protecting a position, that is, to remove yourself from responsibility of any sort for these crimes by saying that you weren't in the line of command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I never said anything that anybody wanted to hear. I always stated my own opinion. This statement of mine or this testimony is not directed against General Halilovic. I'm here to know what I -- to say what I know and to present my point of view. So my testimony from yesterday and my answers today contain only the truth. I have no intention of accusing General Halilovic or anyone else, for that matter. I'm here to tell the truth. I would be happiest if you wished to know if it was proved that General Halilovic is not guilty, even at the price of that, constituting my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I would now seek to show the witness a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, would you just excuse me for a moment, please. I want to explain to the Court and to yourself what is proposed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd seek to show and to tender ultimately a map which is -- would ultimately become a Prosecution exhibit in any event, I believe, but we have the original. This is a map which I'll just display to the Court. It's the original map of the Operation Neretva 93. I would seek that that be placed on a board now so that the witness can refer to it from time to time and the Court and Prosecution can see it. Your Honour, can my co-counsel assist in placing this on the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can it be turned a little so we can also have a view of it from our -- our side of the table, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. But I hope, you know, the camera in this room could pick it up so we could see it on our monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands as to how it should be positioned. I must confess to ignorance as to how the cameras actually function. But what is important is that both the Court and the Prosecutors and also the witness have a chance to see what is there written.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire from the Defence whether this map is any different than the one which is at the back of the room here, the black-and-white one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the quality of the black-and-white one at the back of the room is, and I haven't inspected it, but it looks to be identical. I thank the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusic, I'm going to ask that you be shown some rules concerning the drawing-up and signing of maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P116, the number of which before me is K0111786. This is MFI131, we believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this being a Prosecution document, we are just not sure precisely how this is going to unfold. But any orders or suggestions from those who know, we'll simply accept straight away. I'm going to make a series of apologies to Mr. Gusic and to the Court about this. I just make I want clear that we understand that this inflicts boredom and hardship, so we're apologetic for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, could you please repeat the number that you -- MFI116, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's P116. The MFI number is 131. It hasn't been put forward as yet by the -- by the Prosecution, as we understand. We understand it would be in the Prosecution release documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could be of some assistance to the Defence. We do have it in Sanction, and if it's our exhibit, we could actually display it -- case manager Ana Vrljic could display it on Sanction for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think we have already got it - Am I right - on the screen. The problem is about that, you know, numbering system, you know. I believe that at the beginning of a case it would be some, you know, confusion. I hope later on all of us could get used to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's -- it is something that might take some little time to -- to arrange, and we think it's best rather than seeking adjournments and so on to press on, even though it involves delays and difficulties. If we could seek the Court's leave to press on. I understand that it is difficult for even, but we think we should try. But, however, we are grateful to the Prosecutor so that things can keep moving, we would be -- we would find it acceptable for a document to be put on Sanction. Mr. Gusic could then inspect what he has to inspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We now have -- do you now have in front of you a -- a heading "Chapter IX, combat documents."

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see the English version. Could I see the copy in Bosnian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I'm instructed that you will see it in a minute.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall being shown yesterday one part of this set of rules, being Rule 501?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I'm not going to ask you questions in the abstract. I'll take you to specifics. Now, would you look, please, at -- at Rule 493. And just looking at it while I ask the question - this is a general question - does that section define what are the -- what types of document may be a combat document?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Does it include --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and schemes?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And it's the fact, isn't it, that plans -- sorry, that maps and schemes can in some cases be orders and orders can be communicated in the form of maps and schemes?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders to a lesser degree, but decisions, yes. Orders, no. Basic concepts could be conveyed on a map or on a scheme, but not an order, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I request, since the Prosecution are being extraordinarily helpful here, that they could turn to the next page, where is to be found prong 498.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the moment, I think Mr. Morrissey is under the misapprehension that we are displaying the documents in Sanction. But it is still the Court who is displaying. But we could display them in Sanction if it would be faster for the Court and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I quite understand that. But yesterday Mr. Morrissey made a complaint that his client could not see the B/C/S, so today we'll try our way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I was just being helpful, Your Honours. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Oh, of course. Of course. I just explained the reason why we will try this e-court system at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not have the English version on our screen right now. We now do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Does prong 498 provide as follows? Do you have that again in front of you, Mr. Gusic? Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Does it provide "Orders, demands, directives, instructions and reports contain the following: The name of the command, the time, day, month, year, hour, and place, and issuance in the upper left-hand corner, the confidentiality level and urgency level, section and scope, and year of publication as needed in the upper right-hand corner"? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stated this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I won't trouble you with the -- that may be so, Mr. Gusic. Would you go -- don't worry about the next paragraph, but look at the bottom one: "The following information is placed on plans, maps, tables, or text. The annotation, I have approved it in the upper left-hand corner and position, rank, first name, last name, and the signature of the commanding officer and the time, date -- sorry, the time, date (day, month, year, and hour) of approval is placed below it. The level of confidentiality and registry number is in the upper right-hand corner, the name of the plan and its code name, the section, if needed, in the middle." Is that what's written there?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Although this question may sound funny, because it's going between a -- it's a translation-afflicted question. What's the word that the commander is required to -- to write when -- when that section says "I have approved it" in English? What's the word that is used there in -- in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had it a little bit earlier. The word is "odobravam." This is not written by the person who approved it. It's written by the person who prepares or drafts the document, and then the person who is authorised to approve it then would place their signature there that they approved the order, instruction, concept, or something that is being put to his consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Would you just have a look at that map that's next to you now, please. And for the benefit of the Tribunal, if you could approach the map and read out the words that are to be found in the top left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, I apologise. It may be mechanically difficult to do.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I've seen it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Approved. Armed forces Supreme Command Staff commander, Rasim Delic." Then his personal signature, and a stamp. Let me just look at it. And it's the stamp of the military unit 5001 of the Sarajevo commander. This is the Supreme Command Staff stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusic, Rasim Delic signed that order -- that map as an order in the capacity of commander pursuant to Rule 498, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you completely. This is not an order. This is an idea as to how operations should be conducted. And it was approved. This idea has to be accompanied by the other combat documents, such as an attack command, commands about certain elements of combat security, and a number of commands referring to the solving of specific problems. What we see here is a working map. We see the commander's idea which has been approved, but it is not an order for this to be executed. So the plan has been approved, but the execution has not been ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Isn't that a pure and simple order to carry out those documents -- to carry out those directions that are marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, no. That preparations are to be made in order to act within the framework of this idea or this plan, yes. But we soldiers understand that this is a document that cannot be carried out without a combat order. Such as it is cannot be approved. Whoever approved it would give a great deal of freedom for whoever drew up the plan to write an order different from what was told to him. So this map is not an order. It's simply a plan or an idea for combat operations, an idea that actions should be taken along certain axes and that certain units should be used. But the order itself would have the format that we saw in these rules. That's the only thing you can call an order and a combat document. This is simply an auxiliary document which clarifies matters in graphic and visual terms showing how a certain combat operation can be implemented on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, in the bottom right-hand corner, do you see the signature of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And is the word "nacelnik" to be found there?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was his title.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, when asked by the Prosecutor about the rules of service in the army, I said that up to December 1993 in the Army of BH there were no ranks, only positions. This position had its designation which was used instead of a rank. Today General Halilovic doesn't have to say "chief." He can use his rank, General Halilovic, and sign his name. However, in 1993, when there were no ranks, you had to write what your position was and then sign your name. This was used instead of a rank. His position, Chief of Staff, was used instead of his rank of general or it was closely connected to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You don't dispute that the word "nacelnik" means "Chief of Staff" and is used to designate that function? Perhaps I'll rephrase that, Mr. Gusic, because of the time aspect introduced --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Even before the introduction of ranks, as you've described, that term "nacelnik" meant nothing other than "Chief of Staff" and you understood it to have that meaning; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no, no. Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, he was a superior officer, and we treated him as a superior officer. So it was not just a title, just a post. It carried authority with it, authority which was respected. It fully replaced -- I apologise for my speed. This position -- well, I can't say fully replaced rank because rank carries some other defining elements, but as far as relations in the army went, it fully replaced rank. When it came to duties, assignments, and so on, the function -- or rather, the post, such as a chief, assistant, a deputy, and so on, fully replaced ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So if it's the Prosecution case that Mr. Halilovic was the Chief of Staff of the Bosnian army at this time, you'd say that's a load of rubbish; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no. No, no. It means a lot, sir. It means a lot. He is the second man in the army, the second-ranking general in the army. That means a lot. The number-two man. It still means a lot today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, just to conclude the questions about the formal nature of that map, I put it to you again that that's a decision and an order, not an idea. Do you agree with that or do you maintain your position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't agree with that. This is not an order. This is an idea for the carrying out of combat operations, and this map would have to be accompanied by an order. The map is not an order. It is simply an idea as to how operations can be carried out. It forms part of an order, but it's an incomplete document. I believe that the other part of the document exists, and I would like to see that. Because this was only an attachment to a combat order. Simply one of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So is it your position, Mr. Gusic, that there is another combat order somewhere out there -- well, perhaps I'll withdraw the comment "somewhere out there." I'll start again. Is it your position that there is another combat order signed - just a minute - signed by Commander Delic authorising the launch of what is described there, Operation Neretva? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen it, but I am convinced that General Halilovic would not have launched a combat operation if it did not exist, because he's an experienced soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you that such a document existed at any time before today?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was never something I was very interested in. I was concerned with surviving. I was never engaged in looking into the past. This is the first time I've seen the map as well. I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Didn't the Prosecutor show you the map to get your comments as a experienced -- JNA?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Never?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Didn't the investigator Mr. Mikhailov show it to you at some stage?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Didn't you look at the map when you were consulted about the -- what you've described as the subordination of your units in this operation?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: When the parts of the 44th and 45th Brigade were removed, as you claim, from your control, were you ever shown the map in which operation they were to be used?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say "removed," that's too strong an expression. They were simply separated out for a time and then brought back. I've never seen this map before. I repeat: This is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm going to put some other opportunities to you to see if you remember seeing it on those. What about on the 5th of September at a meeting where the use of 6th Corps units in Operation Neretva 93 was discussed? You didn't see the map at Dobro Polje on the 5th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Commander Delic the night before in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You didn't see --

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. No. And you didn't see this other order to which this map in your account is a mere attachment on either of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't the order that was attached to the map; it was the map that was attached to the order. The order would have to pre-date the map. I didn't see any of it. I never saw the order, and the map, well, today is the first time I've ever seen the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm -- I'll ask you about the order now. I've already mentioned the 44th and the 45th Brigades. From the 6th Corps was also taken the 317th Brigade and the Independent Prozor Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and the Sutjeska Battalion too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I suppose you'd deny Zulfikar's Unit was also taken from you.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing for me to deny. You have a document showing that. There's nothing to deny. You saw that the commander of the 4th Corps commanded certain units and that he commanded Zulfikar's Unit as his.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Has that always been your position, or have you changed that position?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's always been my position. This is the first time I've expressed it as such. I've never said anything else. My position about these special units is something I expressed at the meeting in Zenica, and I asked the commander to reply to my questions about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. In a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you leaving this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, can I indicate I'm going to press him on certain topics, but I'm going to come back to the map from time to time. Might it be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: -- offered at this point, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I believe that it's the proper time for us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think we'll take 20 minutes' break, and when we come back, we'll spend a few minutes on housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've prepared a list for Your Honours so we don't have to go into private session. I'll hand it up. It just has the names of the people on the Defence list and the corresponding numbers on the Prosecution's live witnesses list. The guiding principles in our response to the Defence response are twofold: That is, the role of the Confirming Judge, the Prosecution submits, has been misunderstood by the Defence in its response; and, secondly, the Defence response misunderstands that it is the Prosecution's prerogative how to present its case and which witnesses to call. In relation to the role of the Confirming Judge, the Tribunal's jurisprudence is fairly settled on that, and the most recent pronouncement I can find - there may be more recent ones - was in the Milosevic case when Judge May ruled on the 22nd of November, 2001, the decision on the review of the indictment quoting the test in the Kordic case of Judge McDonald, that is, the decision on the review of the indictment of the 10th of November, 1995, adopting, as other Trial Chambers have, Her Honour's pronouncement that: "A prima facie case for this purpose is understood to be a credible case which would, if not contradicted by the Defence, be a sufficient basis to convict the accused on the charge." When the Prosecution submitted its confirming materials to Judge Wald in -- sorry, in 2001, it did so with a covering letter informing Her Honour that the matter was -- was being referred to the Trial Chamber, subject to continuing investigations. The indictment was therefore confirmed on the basis that the Prosecution's investigations were ongoing. Her Honour was satisfied on the material, the 109 statement which is were put before Her Honour that there was a prima facie case in relation to the indictment which, as the Trial Chamber understands, has remained unchanged. To be quite frank, hindsight is a wonderful thing. If anything, the Prosecution probably put too many statements before Judge Wald in 2001. And there is much overlap between the statements of the witnesses upon which Her Honour confirmed the indictment. And at some point the case has to be severely -- or the witness list has to be cut back to make it manageable for Prosecution, Defence, and Trial Chamber, given the nature of what this case is in the context of proceedings before the Tribunal. It's a much smaller case in scope, and the number of witnesses that should be called, live or by 98 bis, had to be drastically reduced. And the Prosecution has done this several times and most recently, and quite frankly, most ruthlessly in December -- mid-December when we were aware that a trial -- when we became aware that a trial date was going -- was very, very imminent, and we went through every witness who was on the list and we compared all the statements to try and eliminate all -- as much repetition as we could and to put forward what we considered the most credible and reliable evidence, that is, the best evidence we thought we could put from the statements before the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution -- our submission is that there is no prejudice to the Defence here by our application to reduce the witness list. If anything, it should help the Defence in their presentation of their case -- sorry, in their defence to the Prosecution case. And if anything, the Defence application, if it is based upon the fact that Judge Wald confirmed the indictment and seven of the eight witnesses on the list which I've handed up to Your Honours were on that list - the only one who wasn't is number 6 - were before Judge Wald. She confirmed it on that basis. The prima facie case existed because there were so many statements. Take these away and the prima facie case doesn't exist. It's illogical for the Defence to say that we should call these witnesses. Because if the Defence submission is now there's no prima facie case as a result, that would become fairly clear and one would think at the Rule 98 bis statement Mr. Halilovic will walk free because the case -- there could be no prima facie case on that submission. So the Prosecution doesn't understand the logic in that line -- in that line of thought. Now, the reason why we cut -- or we have sought to cut these witnesses is because of the repetition, the overlap. And if I could briefly address Your Honours -- and I'll just give you the numbers on the Prosecution list to compare against the numbers on the Defence list. In relation to Witness 1 on the Defence list, Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the revised one, 2, 11 -- I apologise for that. 15, 20, and 21. We say cover anything witness -- Defence witness number 1 could cover. Those same numbers apply to Witness 2 on the Defence list and Witness 8 on the Defence list. Further, on -- in relation to Witness 3 on the Defence list, Prosecution Witnesses 11 and 28 cover the same territory. In relation to Witness 4 on the Defence list, Prosecution Witness 6 covers that. Defence Witness number 5, an HVO soldier; the Prosecution is calling Witnesses 33 and 34, also HVO soldiers who cover the same territory. Witness number 6, the Prosecution intends -- or seeks leave to call Witness 27, who corroborates the taking of the statement to which he would be called. Number 7 on the Defence list; Prosecution Witness number 12 covers it same ground. In fact, in some of these we are calling the witness's superior or someone in the same chain of command who can cover the identical issue of the failure to investigate or what should have been -- what should have been done. And there is no benefit to the Trial Chamber or judicial economy to -- for calling multiple witnesses to cover the same points. Witness number 2 and Witness number 8 on the Defence list both informed the Prosecution investigates and senior trial -- former senior trial attorney at the end of 2003 that they did not wish to give evidence for the Prosecution. That was a further factor in our consideration of choosing them -- sorry, choosing other witnesses instead of them. In relation to Witness number 2, that information is contradicted by a letter the Defence filed with their motion in which he said that he would come. We've had conflicting information. But in relation to -- in Witness number 8 on the Defence list, he said clearly in the letter which is filed with the Defence motion, "I do not wish to testify against Sefer Halilovic because I am of the view that he is not guilty and that I do not have any arguments that would show that he is guilty." Now, Your Honours should be completely satisfied with that. But there is no reason why the Prosecutor would call someone who on the face of the letter the Defence filed is hostile to the Prosecution case. There will be no benefit in us calling him and seeking leave to have him declared hostile when we have five other witnesses we say who cover the same territory. There are, of course, other avenues available to the Defence if they feel they want to have these witness who is they say confirm the prima facie case against their client called, that is, to seek the Trial Chamber's leave to have the Trial Chamber call the witnesses if it becomes -- if the Trial Chamber feels that it is necessary after having heard the Prosecution case or, secondly, to call the witnesses themselves. The Prosecution submits -- my final point is there is no prejudice to the Defence and they -- the onus is on the Defence to demonstrate the prejudice and it would have to be fairly significant prejudice to -- to demonstrate -- sorry, to interfere -- to ask the Trial Chamber to interfere with the Prosecution's prerogative to call the witnesses it says are most relevant to the case and to conduct the case in the manner in which the Prosecution desires. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one question to you, Mr. Re: The seven new witnesses' statement has already been furnished to the Defence, I guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I don't have that information at my fingertips. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But you're definitely sure that the statements have been furnished to the Defence team already?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm very, very certain of that. And I'm sure my learned friend will be on his feet if it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Please be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will be extremely concise. First, concerning the issue of the statements of the seven new proposed witnesses. It would appear on the face of it that we have indeed received all of the statements of those seven persons. Concerning the other issues raised by the Prosecution, I think you asked us quite -- two quite clear questions yesterday. The first one was: Which one of the eight witnesses which the Defence insists should not be withdrawn from the Prosecution list were put before the Confirming Judge. And the answer is a simple one; it is all of them. Concerning the second issue raised by Your Honour yesterday as to the importance of those witnesses to the Prosecution case, the answer is, I believe, equally simple. It would suffice to skim through the original Prosecution pre-trial brief and look at the footnotes which the Prosecution used in those pre-trial briefs. And one would find that the two most-often quoted or cited witnesses are Mr. Bilajac and Mr. Suljevic. In the order of most-often quoted witnesses, one would also find the rest of those eight witnesses. The Defence wants to make it clear that it does not claim to be prejudiced by the shortening of the list in itself, and quite the contrary, as the Prosecution pointed out. But the Defence believes and has made it clear in its submissions that it is in the interest of justice, the Defence would submit that, those witnesses should still be called - and I'm talking about the eight witnesses - should be called by the Prosecution. For the rest, Your Honour, I would simply direct your attention to our submission of the 29th of December. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Well, Mr. Mettraux, there is also a question to you, that is: Is there any possibility that the Defence team could call that eight witnesses in your defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is certainly a possibility for the Defence to do so, but there are a number of issues. First, some of those witnesses may be hostile to the Defence, may refuse to come if so requested by the Defence. The other matter is the Defence would have obviously to examine them in chief and the Prosecution to cross-examine them, and the Defence want to make it quite clear that that material which those witnesses provided to the Prosecution at the time was put before the Confirming Judge and was a fundamental - fundamental - base on which the indictment was confirmed. And I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that from the order confirming the indictment it would appear that the first attempt by the Prosecution to have an indictment confirmed against Mr. Halilovic was refused in July 2001 and there was a further resubmission of the indictment in September when it was confirmed. We would like to make that point quite clear. But to answer Your Honour's question, yes, that is a possibility, for us to call those witnesses. There may be a problem, there may be refusal, and we would obviously be in favour of the proposals that we've put forward; namely, the Prosecution be ordered to call those who are still are their witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe that the picture is more clear than before, so we'll render our rulings as early as possible. I hope today, but I'm not quite sure. And anyway, at the beginning of the next week there will be a written decision to this effect. Having said that, could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, are you ready to start, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I apologise for that later delay, because we had some housekeeping matters to do. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Just excuse me for a moment, please, while I find what I wanted to put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gusic, you indicated yesterday and -- that -- as to the status of the Zulfikar Unit, that that had become resubordinated to the 4th Corps. Now you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not become resubordinated, but it became part of the composition of the 4th Corps. There is a difference. It became an organic part of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. But the fact of the matter is that whatever orders to that effect may have been drafted by General Delic -- sorry, I withdraw that -- by Rasim Delic and by Arif Pasalic, I put it to you that as a matter of practice that transfer simply never happened at all. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. If you have an order by Arif Pasalic that Zulfikar Alispago becomes the commander of the Sjever OG, how could that command have been implemented or been taken into account unless the unit had become an organic part of the corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I put to you that you in the past have recognised that that transfer never in fact took place. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that either. Because there was communication between the commander, Zulfikar Alispago, and the late Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Gusic, I want to put something to you from an interview that you had at the cantonal court in Sarajevo in 19 -- just excuse me. I'll put to you the proper date -- on the 11th -- sorry, on the 11th of March, 1999. Did you say this on that occasion, at page 3: "To tell the truth" -- sorry, I take that back. I'll read you another sentence. "For the purpose of the execution of the" --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We don't -- can we see what particular document he's referring to, please. We don't have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends how long that document will be quoted. Maybe just one sentence. We'll let Mr. Morrissey go and to see whether there's a need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: To assist the Prosecutor, can I indicate that it's -- it's from the statement that I quoted, provided to us by the Prosecution, and I'm going to read about six lines followed by about three more lines subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Mr. Gusic. Now I'll read to you the preliminary sentence followed by what comes: "For the purpose of the execution of the combat activities, besides the units deployed to carry out the combat tasks, the forward command post established the unit, that is, the Zulfikar special purposes detachment of the Supreme Command Staff, under the command of the brigadier, Zulfikar Alispago. To tell the truth, the unit was also a part of the 6th Corps under my command, but during the execution of planned combat activities the unit was under the command of the forward command post. Senior officers of the forward command post were giving war combat assignments to this unit. Therefore, the unit was obliged to fulfil tasks given by the commander of the forward command post." Now, Mr. Gusic, it's the fact, isn't it, that on that occasion you were acknowledging that Zulfikar's Unit was under the 6th Corps, albeit having been resubordinated to the IKM, and you didn't refer to the 4th Corps resubordination in the least; correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated this yesterday, and I don't want to say anything that wasn't true. Under the organisational structure, there was a unit under the command of Zulfikar. And the reason why I requested the commander to resolve the status of that unit at the advisory meeting in Zenica was precisely because I wasn't commanding that unit. I'm not trying to say that it wasn't within the composition. It was, until the order that the commander issued, and it was sent there. After that, Zulfikar's Unit was in the -- in the composition of the 4th Corps. I never at any point claimed it was not part of it but practically it wasn't because I never actually assumed command of that unit, and I stated that before and I will continue to say it. And I said the same thing before that court. I stated it probably in the way you read it out. But the gist is as I have just explained it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, let's just be clear, in fairness to you. What you're saying is that the Zulfikar Unit was originally, in theory, under the 6th Corps, although it was not necessarily within the line of command and control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was essential. I wouldn't like to -- like to assess that. But when the organisational decisions were made, probably there was a need for that. There is an order stating when the corps was formed, that the special purpose unit was part of the 6th Corps. It's true that out in the field it was never part of the 6th Corps; it was always directly linked to the Supreme Command Staff. And I did put the question about the status amongst other things, not only of that unit but other special units at the advisory meeting in Zenica, and it's true that after that the commander resolved the status of that unit by deploying it as part of the organic composition of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Gusic, just -- perhaps my questions are not perfect. And I apologise for that. But your position is this. I'll summarise it and you tell me if that's right. You say that the Zulfikar Unit was transferred by Delic to the command of the 4th Corps and that thereafter the commander of the 4th Corps resubordinated it to the IKM? Is that your position now?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you saw those documents, so I cannot tell you anything else than what has been shown over the past couple of days. Yes, that was so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. The answer is yes. All right. Well, in the statement I was reading out to you before, did you go on to say this: "Regarding the combat tasks, this unit under the command of the forward command post was responsible for execution of combat activities to the commander of the forward command post. The unit was part of the 6th Corps, and as commander of the 6th Corps, I was still authorised to provide logistical help to the unit. That was the 6th Corps's permanent activity that could not have been stopped." Did you say in the statement to the cantonal court in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second part regarding logistics referred to all of the units which were engaged in the mentioned operation, so the need for logistics did not stop when the -- I don't know about the Zulfikar Unit. I am not claiming that we did not perform logistics functions for them as well. There were things that I could provide from Konjic or Jablanica or from the area of responsibility from the 6th Corps, but that could also come from Brdo or over the mountains. But I'm categorically stating that that unit was not part of the 6th Corps during the combat operations. I think the report that you've read out to me, it's six years old. I find it very difficult to remember things. I remember what I had for lunch yesterday but not for the day before. It's very hard to remember what I said 20 minutes ago, never mind six years ago. But the essence of what I said is the following: The Zulfikar Unit was not an organic part of the 6th Corps. As far as logistics are concerned - fuel, and ammunition, possibly communications equipment, food - that is probably something that did happen, so I cannot remember that we did or didn't carry out these functions for them. There probably were such activities on our part, but that does not mean or -- that they were in the chain of command, even if we did perform such functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, have a look at that big map behind you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I ask Mr. Gusic to do that, might I tender that map. I think I started to do so before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecution also tendered the similar maps which is a copy of this map. Do we have to tender it twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure that that map was tendered. Although there's a copy leaning over there, I don't think that was one of the two. My recollection is that they tendered the big regional map that had the -- which you can see behind the black and white Neretva 93 over there. And that they also tendered the standard Bosnian map, which is tendered in many cases. I think that's the fact. My friend can confirm that, if that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position about the map is, I used it in the opening, but when I did ask for my learned counsel whether he objects for it to be tendered into evidence, he had objected at that point. So that is why it's not tendered. But if he no longer has that objection, of course we have no objection for it to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, many times I'm unclear. I'm sorry to the Prosecutor, because I didn't mean to oppose them tendering that map into evidence. I've got no doubt I expressed myself that way, but in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on which stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If you know in the opening stage, well, usually that the Trial Chamber does not admit any documents at that stage. But now we are in the trial stage. I think, you know, the parties are free, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- You know, to tender any documents into evidence. By my question is that: The map used by the Prosecution and the map tendered by you today, are they the same map?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I -- well, what I can say is that map there was acquired by the Defence and we think it's the original map, and it's likely that the Prosecution one is a -- a better but only a copy. And, therefore, we'd seek the tender the original map as we understand it to be. It's better because it's in colour and it's -- it would be more helpful to the Chamber and quite frankly more helpful to witnesses, especially if it should happen to prove, Your Honour, that any witnesses actually saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Because we only have the black-and-white map. I stand to be corrected. But that is my understanding. So therefore we are quite happy to have that one in colour because that is a photocopy of this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So this document is admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gusic. Now, would you mind, after that, have a look at the map, please, and indicate where on that map you see signified the IKM forward command post at which the Prosecution and you say the -- was the command post for Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that the IKM is marked anywhere, or at least the usual symbol was not used that would indicate a forward command post. I don't see the brigade command posts either. I don't see the IKM command post. I don't see any of the command posts. So that element of the combat order has not been marked. That is why I told you a little earlier that this is not an order, that it's a concept or an idea for operations and it must be accompanied by an order. Here you just have access of operations. This document is not an order and does not have all the elements that an order is supposed to have. One of the elements of an order, of course, are all the positions of the command posts. And, again, I claim that this is only an idea or a concept for a combat operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Or is the answer, the other one, that there's no forward command post marked on there because there really was no forward command post and the commander was Commander Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please, please, I would like to be fair, so please don't make me give you the wrong answer. Can you claim that I wasn't at the forward command post? I know I'm not in a position to ask questions, but I personally was at the forward command post of the Supreme Command Staff in Jablanica and I was at the thermoelectric power station. I was there personally once, perhaps even twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, what we're going to put to you is that not only did you go to the Jablanica power station for a meeting but you attended at numerous meetings because you played an important part in Operation Neretva 93. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that I was there many times. I could have been there two to three times at the most at the forward command post. I was not an important person in the Neretva 93 operation because I was not familiar with the plan of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Gusic, you're certainly going to have an opportunity to answer questions about that in due course. Can I indicate to you now that -- I'm going to ask you some questions about a brief chronology, just to locate some of the other matters that are going to be the subject of questioning. And then I'm going to take you to particular instances broadly in a chronological order and that may assist to know where the questions are aimed at so that you can understand what -- what is being put. As to a very broad chronology, can I just ask you whether the following facts are right? And this might assist the Court as well. Is it the fact that you and all the other corps commanders attended at Zenica for a meeting of corps commanders on the 22nd -- sorry, 21st and 22nd of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the week after that, was there considerable activity by the HVO of a hostile kind on the front line in Herzegovina and particularly in the vicinity of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SALKO GUSIC [Resumed]
